title: India's Private Banks Bet Big on Corporate Loans as Bond Market Loses Its Edge
excerpt: Top private lenders posted double-digit loan growth in Q1 FY27 as companies swap bonds for cheaper bank credit, but a widening deposit gap and margin pressure cloud the outlook.
body:
• India's top private banks posted loan growth of 12-18% year-on-year in Q1 FY27, with corporate credit emerging as the primary growth engine alongside resilient retail and MSME lending.
  • Companies are swapping bond financing for bank loans as bond market yields make bank credit comparatively cheaper, giving private lenders a pricing advantage.
  • HDFC Bank's deposits grew 14.7% and advances 15.4% year-on-year, while Yes Bank reported a 34% profit jump to ₹10.7 billion, driven by 18.3% loan growth.
  • Margin pressure is building as low-cost CASA deposits decline and banks rely more on expensive wholesale funding, with NIMs expected to contract 5-10 basis points sequentially.

Corporate Credit Comes Back

India's private banks are riding a corporate loan revival that marks a significant shift in the country's credit landscape. After years of cautious lending and stressed asset cleanup, private lenders are aggressively expanding their corporate loan books as companies increasingly choose bank credit over bond market financing.

Systemic credit growth hit 17.7% year-on-year by mid-June, according to Motilal Oswal, supported by stronger corporate borrowing, resilient retail demand, and continued momentum in MSME and gold loans. Loans to the private corporate sector grew 15.5% as of March 2026, up sharply from 11.9% a year earlier, according to the Reserve Bank of India's annual statistical report.

Q1 Results Signal Momentum

Provisional numbers from India's largest private lenders confirm the trend. HDFC Bank, the country's biggest private bank, reported deposit growth of 14.7% and gross advance growth of 15.4% year-on-year. Kotak Mahindra Bank's net advances rose 15.1%, while Yes Bank posted a 34% profit surge to ₹10.7 billion on the back of 18.3% loan growth and a net interest margin expansion to 2.7%.

JM Financial's analysis of 28 banks showed aggregate loan growth of roughly 16.4% year-on-year, with private banks expected to outpace public sector lenders. Motilal Oswal forecasts an earnings compound annual growth rate of about 20.5% for private banks, compared with 9.6% for state-owned lenders.

"We estimate banks to post around 12% to 13% loan growth in FY2027, aided by steady growth in retail and MSME loans and improvement in corporate loans."

— Vishal Narnolia, ICICI Securities

The Bond Market Shift

A key driver of the corporate loan boom is a pricing shift away from bond markets. As bond yields have hardened, the cost advantage that large Indian corporates once enjoyed through direct market borrowing has narrowed. Bloomberg reported that Indian firms are swapping bonds for cheaper bank loans, particularly as the RBI's rate-cutting cycle has made bank credit more attractive for corporate treasurers.

The easing of liquidity coverage ratio norms has also freed up an estimated ₹2.7-3 lakh crore in lendable resources, giving banks more firepower to compete for corporate mandates.

Deposit Gap Raises Concerns

The growth story has a significant caveat: deposits are not keeping pace. Across the banking system, credit growth is outpacing deposit mobilization, pushing credit-deposit ratios higher and forcing banks to rely on more expensive wholesale funding.

HDFC Bank's low-cost CASA deposit share slipped to 32.35% from 33.9% a year earlier. The trend is systemic. Sequential NIM compression of 5-10 basis points is expected in Q1, according to JM Financial, driven by stronger growth in lower-yield corporate lending and higher-cost certificates of deposit.

Motilal Oswal expects sharper margin pressure on mid-sized private lenders, with AU Small Finance Bank facing around 13 basis points of NIM contraction and Bandhan Bank about 10 basis points.

What NRI Investors Should Watch

For the Indian diaspora with investments in banking stocks, the picture is nuanced. The corporate loan revival is a genuine growth lever that should drive earnings, particularly for HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, and Axis Bank. But the deposit crunch and margin compression mean that revenue growth may not flow through to profits as cleanly as in previous cycles.

Asset quality remains stable, with gross non-performing assets projected below 2.1% in FY27. But private banks may report higher slippages than public sector lenders due to their greater exposure to unsecured and MSME portfolios. Investors should watch the CASA trajectory and the pace of the RBI's rate-cutting cycle, which will determine whether deposit costs stabilize or continue climbing.
